title: CHAPTER TEN. On the Gospel: definition
english: CHAPTER TEN. On the Gospel: where also on the Apostles' Creed.

The Gospel is the word of God announcing and proposing to all humans Christ the Redeemer with His merits to be apprehended, and freely promising to those who apprehend Him by living faith remission of sins, righteousness, and eternal salvation for His sake.

Gospel properly means a good or glad message. In theology it notes the good news of the Savior born for us (Luke 2:10-11) and His merits; specially the doctrine of Christ the Redeemer and free remission of sins for Him (Matt. 11:5; Rom. 1:16). Sometimes it sometimes refers to the whole New Testament teaching, which also embraces the law (Mark 1:14-15).

title: Matter of the Gospel: Christ and application of His merit
english: The Gospel chiefly contains as subject-matter two things: 1. the doctrine of Christ the Savior of humans and His merit (Rom. 1:3)—incarnation, fulfillment of the law, payment of penalties, liberation from the curse, reconciliation with God, overthrow of the Devil;
2. the doctrine of applying Christ's merit—remission of sins (Acts 10:36, 43), perfect righteousness of Christ promised to us (1 Cor. 1:30), and eternal salvation (Rom. 1:16; 1 Tim. 1:15).

title: Differences between Law and Gospel
english: Law and Gospel differ: 1. in matter—the law commands works; the Gospel announces Christ to be apprehended by faith (Rom. 3:27; Gal. 3:2);
2. in form—law-promises under condition of one's own merit (Lev. 18:5); Gospel-promises free (Rom. 4:16; Eph. 2:8);
3. in effects—the law terrifies and condemns (Rom. 3:20); the Gospel consoles and absolves (Isa. 61:1-2; Luke 4:18);
4. in object—the law toward the ungodly; the Gospel toward crushed hearts (Matt. 11:28);
5. in mode of revelation—the law somehow known by nature (Rom. 2:15); the Gospel a mystery revealed through the Son (John 1:18; Rom. 16:26).

title: Gospel is not a doctrine of works; summa is the Apostles' Creed
english: Therefore the Gospel is not a doctrine of works, and so adds neither new commands nor counsels upon the divine law. That it is not a doctrine of works is clear from Romans 10.

III. The compendium or little sum of the Gospel is the Apostles' Creed, whose letter, origin, and authority are to be considered. IV. Its letter, harmoniously arranged, the following SCHEMA of the sum exhibits.

title: V–VII. Origin of the Creed: baptismal Trinity; later expansions against heresies
english: V–VII. From the beginning the baptismal Creed consisted in the Trinity alone, as gathered from the earliest fathers and the Nicene Creed. Ancient expositions do not go beyond the Trinity.

VII. What the Creed is today, as to the remaining clauses, contains nothing but as if in splendid garments and fair structures built upon that foundation, which in their times were necessarily added to extinguish heresies and are now necessarily retained lest they break out again. Heretics gave occasion for a more popular explanation of that Creed which before had been folded as in majesty of silence.

title: VIII–IX. Authority of the Creed; Cap.11 next
english: VIII. The authority of the Apostles' Creed is considered either as it was from the beginning, or as it was later explained on the occasion of diverse heresies.

IX. The authority of the Creed as it was from the beginning is altogether divine and equal to the other canonical Scriptures, for it is immediately from Jesus Christ our Savior (Matt. 28:19). Among juniors Luther, Melanchthon, Erasmus, Bullinger, Calvin, Chytraeus, Hemmingius, Ursinus, Olevianus, Piscator, Perkins, Alsted, and others have piously and learnedly expounded the sense of the articles.
